answers.q1: I joined in 1992 as a graduate trainee drilling engineer on land rigs in Ankleshwar and spent my first decade learning that rig-floor discipline is the foundation of everything. Offshore postings in Mumbai High followed, and I moved from rig supervision to planning and eventually to heading Drilling Services. The defining moment was my first well control event as a young engineer. It taught me that procedures exist because someone once paid for ignoring them.
answers.q2: Our toughest problem was repeated stuck pipe in high-angle extended-reach wells through a depleted carbonate section. The root cause was equivalent circulating density exceeding the fracture gradient of a weak zone, causing losses and then hole packoff. We revised the mud programme with lower rheology, added real-time pressure monitoring and set trip speed limits. Non-productive time on that campaign fell by about a third.
answers.q3: My biggest failure was accepting a vendor's bit recommendation without validating it against offset well data. We lost two bit runs and about four days of rig time. Since then I insist on an offset well review and a written justification before any change in drilling parameters or consumables.
answers.q4: Never normalise a flow check that does not look right. Every crew member must have stop-work authority and use it without fear. Hold kick drills seriously, because the crew that practises in calm weather responds correctly in a real kick. Verify BOP test records yourself instead of relying only on the summary sheet.
answers.q5: If mud returns change colour or the pit level creeps up even slightly during a connection, stop and investigate before pulling further. Trust trends over single readings. Most problems announce themselves hours earlier in torque and drag trends.
answers.q6: My first mentor was a toolpusher on a land rig in Ankleshwar who made me stand every night tour for a month before he let me sign a tour report. He taught me to ask the crew before asking the manual. I have tried to pass that on by pairing every new drilling engineer with a driller for six months, and by writing a one-page 'what we would do differently' note after each well that the next team must read before spudding.
answers.q7: I am handing over three things. First, a campaign to standardise well control training and drills across all offshore rigs, which is about two thirds complete. Second, a real-time monitoring centre that still needs better alarm rationalisation so that crews do not learn to ignore alerts. Third, a bench of young rig managers who are technically strong but need more exposure to contractor negotiations. The main risk is complacency after several years without a serious well control event.
answers.q8: Spend your first three years on the rig, not behind a desk. Learn from the driller and the toolpusher, who carry decades of tacit knowledge. Keep your own notebook and share what you learn.

answers.q1: I joined in 1991 as a graduate engineer in production and was posted to Cambay, where I worked on rod-pumped wells and later on workovers and stimulation. Over the years I moved into well services planning, covering coiled tubing, hydraulic fracturing and wireline. The defining moment was leading my first large fracturing job in a tight reservoir, where careful pre-job design made the difference between a dry hole and a producer.
answers.q2: Our toughest job was restoring a cluster of sand-choked wells in a mature Cambay field. We moved from conventional workovers to coiled tubing sand washing with nitrogen assist, which cut job time from nine days to three. The result was recovery of several wells that had been written off.
answers.q3: I once rushed a coiled tubing job to use a weather window and skipped a full function test of the nitrogen unit. The pump failed mid-job and we lost the window and a day of crew time anyway. I now insist on complete equipment checks at the yard and again on location, and I tell crews that a delayed start is always cheaper than a stopped job.
answers.q4: Pressure is the main hazard in well services. Every connection must be pressure tested to the programme value with everybody clear of the line. Barriers must be known and written on the job board before any intervention. Respect hydrogen sulphide and flammable gas, and never allow ignition sources near a flowing well. Brief the whole crew on the emergency shutdown, who presses what, and where to muster.
answers.q5: Before any intervention, read the well history in reverse: start with the last three jobs, not the completion diagram. Repeated problems at the same depth usually have a single root cause nobody has written down.
answers.q6: I learnt my craft from a senior wireline supervisor who believed that a good engineer should be able to do every task on the crew. He made me run the winch and rig up the lubricator myself. I have kept that spirit by organising skill clinics where engineers and crew teach each other, and by writing every unusual job up as a short case note for the whole department.
answers.q7: I am handing over a programme to move from conventional workovers to rigless interventions in mature Cambay wells, which still needs a second coiled tubing unit. I am also leaving a backlog of sand-control candidates ranked by value. The main risk is that experienced crews are retiring faster than new ones can be trained, so the training pipeline needs to start now.
answers.q8: Be curious about why a well behaves the way it does, not only about how to fix it. Spend time with the production and reservoir teams, because the best interventions come from combining their views. Keep a personal logbook of jobs, and share failures as openly as successes, since that is how a department gets better.

answers.q1: I began as a reservoir engineer at the Dehradun institute, working on material balance for small onshore pools, and later led integrated studies for large offshore carbonate fields. The turning point was realising that a simulation model is only as good as the surveillance data feeding it. I spent years building the habit of regular pressure surveys and well tests.
answers.q2: Our hardest problem was declining pressure and early water breakthrough in a mature carbonate reservoir. We re-interpreted the injection pattern, shifted injectors to improve sweep and balanced voidage replacement across layers. Oil decline slowed from about eight percent a year to roughly four percent.
answers.q3: I once trusted a history match that reproduced production beautifully but ignored an inconsistent pressure survey. The forecast over-predicted by almost twenty percent and an infill programme was sized on it. I now insist that a model must match pressures as well as rates, and that an independent team challenges it before any investment decision.
answers.q4: In reservoir work the safety lesson is about decisions that put people at risk indirectly. Never size a facility, a platform load or water handling capacity on an optimistic forecast, because operations will then be forced to run equipment beyond its limits. Share the uncertainty range openly with operations and HSE colleagues, and revisit it after every surveillance campaign.
answers.q5: Always check voidage replacement ratio before trusting any forecast. If injection and withdrawal do not balance, the model is telling you a story the field does not agree with. I also plot water-oil ratio against cumulative production on a log scale because slope changes show channelling early.
answers.q6: My guide was a senior reservoir engineer who made me hand-plot every pressure survey on graph paper for a year before touching a simulator. He said you only feel the reservoir when you plot it yourself. I pass this on through a study circle where juniors present a field to the group each month and are questioned by geologists, petrophysicists and production engineers together.
answers.q7: I am handing over a polymer flood pilot that needs two more years of data before the economics are clear, and an under-used history-matching workflow that can speed up studies. The risk is that surveillance budgets get cut when oil prices dip. That is exactly when data matters most.
answers.q8: Learn the whole chain from geology to the export pipeline, not only your own software. Question every number, including your own, and always ask what would change your mind. Read old reports from your field, because many of today's surprises were noted decades ago by someone who did not have the tools to act.

answers.q1: I started as a logging engineer in Vadodara, running wireline units in the field. I learnt early that no interpretation can rescue a badly acquired log. Over thirty years I moved from the logging unit to log quality control and then to heading logging services, covering open-hole, cased-hole and production logging. The defining moment was seeing a bad calibration lead to a wrong water saturation and an unnecessary completion test, which taught me that quality control belongs at the wellsite, not in the office.
answers.q2: The toughest challenge was evaluating thin laminated sand-shale sequences where conventional resistivity logs read too low and the pay was being missed. We introduced high-resolution image logs and a laminated-sand analysis workflow, and recalibrated the cut-offs with core data. Several zones that had been written off were tested and produced, adding meaningful reserves to the field.
answers.q3: I once accepted a tool run in a washed-out hole without insisting on a repeat pass, and the density log was unreliable across a key interval. We lost confidence in the zone and had to run a costly cased-hole evaluation later. I now require a repeat section and a caliper review before the tool leaves the hole.
answers.q4: Radioactive sources and explosives demand absolute discipline. Source handling must follow the procedure every time, with barriers, signage and a trained source custodian. Radio silence rules for perforating must be respected on every job. If a tool is stuck, stop and call for help instead of improvising, because a fishing job with a source in the hole is a high-risk operation.
answers.q5: Read the calipers before the curves, because a rugose hole explains many strange readings. Check that the density-neutron separation makes geological sense, and compare resistivity curves across depths of investigation to spot invasion. If a log looks too good, ask what could make it look that way before celebrating.
answers.q6: My mentor was a senior logging engineer who made me sit through his quality control sessions before every job was released. I now run monthly log review clinics where field engineers, petrophysicists and geologists look at the same log together, and I make sure juniors present their own interpretations to seniors.
answers.q7: I am handing over a logging-while-drilling data quality programme that is half complete, and a plan to replace ageing wireline units with units that have better telemetry. The risk is that experienced logging engineers are retiring, so the calibration and quality control know-how must be written down and taught soon.
answers.q8: Go to the wellsite and stay through a full logging job. Learn how the tool works, what its limits are and what the driller sees. Never interpret a log without asking how it was acquired, and make friends with the geologists, because a good interpretation is always a team effort.

answers.q1: I joined as a geophysicist working on land seismic crews in Cambay and later moved into processing and interpretation centres. Over three decades I saw the industry move from analogue records to full-waveform workstations. The constant was that the best interpreters understood how the data was acquired.
answers.q2: Our toughest challenge was imaging beneath a thick basalt cover where conventional seismic gave poor reflections. We designed long-offset, low-frequency acquisition and tested multiple velocity model strategies. The improved image allowed us to define a drillable prospect that earlier data had hidden.
answers.q3: I once approved a processing flow without checking the velocity model against well checkshot data. The depth conversion was off by tens of metres and the well missed its target. Now I always tie seismic to wells before releasing any depth map.
answers.q4: Seismic crews work in remote terrain with explosives, heavy vehicles and long days. Fatigue and journey management are the biggest dangers, so never allow a driver to run beyond safe hours. Explosive handling must follow the licence conditions exactly. In offshore surveys respect fishing community and marine life protocols, and keep the permit and emergency plan on board at all times.
answers.q5: If a seismic section looks too clean, ask what the processor did to it. Always look at the raw shot gathers and a minimally processed stack before accepting a pretty migrated image. Check that multiples have been addressed in shallow water, and compare amplitudes against well data before trusting any attribute.
answers.q6: I was fortunate to work under a processing geophysicist who made us explain every parameter we chose. I now run an annual workshop where interpreters visit the processing centre and processors visit the field, so each side understands the other's constraints. Young geoscientists present a prospect to a challenge panel every quarter.
answers.q7: I am handing over a full-waveform inversion project for the basalt-covered area, which has promising early results, and a plan to reprocess legacy seismic with modern algorithms. The risk is that legacy tapes are deteriorating, so data preservation and digitisation must continue to receive funding.
answers.q8: Go to the field at least once and watch a seismic crew work. Understand noise, permits and terrain. Then you will know why a gap in coverage exists and what it means for your interpretation.

answers.q1: I started as a production engineer on an offshore process platform and gradually moved to managing surface operations across several assets. Production is the one function where you meet the consequences of every upstream decision. I learnt to walk the platform every day and listen to the equipment.
answers.q2: Our worst problem was wax deposition and separator carry-over on a platform with declining flow rates. We introduced regular pigging, optimised chemical injection and improved separator internals. Unplanned shutdowns dropped by roughly forty percent over two years.
answers.q3: I once approved a temporary bypass of a high-level trip on a separator to avoid a shutdown during a production push. A slug arrived, liquid carried over into the gas line and a compressor was damaged. The repair cost far exceeded the production we had protected. I now treat every trip bypass as a formal decision with a written risk assessment and a time limit.
answers.q4: Never bypass a safety system for production, even for one hour. Isolations, permits to work and shift handovers must be written and read aloud. Most serious incidents I investigated had a missing or misunderstood handover.
answers.q5: A change in the sound of a compressor or a slight temperature drift on a separator is usually the first warning. Keep an operator's logbook habit even in the age of dashboards. Trends on paper often reveal what alarms miss.
answers.q6: My mentor was an offshore installation manager who walked every deck with me at dawn and asked me to explain what each valve did. I run similar walkdowns with young production engineers, and I ask each of them to teach a colleague one system every month so that they truly understand it.
answers.q7: I am handing over a project to upgrade produced water treatment, which is critical to meet discharge norms, and a plan to retrofit older platforms with remote monitoring. The risk is ageing pipelines and separators, so inspection and corrosion management budgets must be protected.
answers.q8: Learn the process from wellhead to export, and learn it on the platform. Make friends with operators and maintenance technicians, because they notice problems first. Treat every shutdown as a chance to learn and write down what you found, because the next engineer will need it.

answers.q1: I joined in 1993 as a graduate mechanical engineer and began on offshore platform maintenance, working with pumps, compressors and turbines. Over three decades I moved into reliability engineering, overhaul planning and then heading the mechanical function. The defining moment was leading a major overhaul during the monsoon, which taught me that planning, spares and teamwork matter more than any individual skill.
answers.q2: Repeated bearing failures on a gas compressor train threatened a platform's export. Vibration analysis showed misalignment caused by pipe strain from a recent modification. We corrected the supports, re-aligned the train and added online vibration monitoring. The train has since run for over two years without a bearing failure.
answers.q3: I once deferred an overhaul to meet a production target. The machine failed in service, costing far more than the planned shutdown. I now treat condition-based overhaul triggers as non-negotiable and explain the cost of deferral to management with numbers.
answers.q4: Never work on a machine that has not been properly isolated, locked out and tested for zero energy. Respect stored energy in springs, pressurised lines and rotating shafts. Confirm lifting plans and certificates before any heavy lift, and never stand under a load. Near-miss reports on rotating equipment should be shared with every crew in the same week.
answers.q5: Touch the casing and listen to the machine before you read the screen. Trend vibration, bearing temperature and lube oil pressure together, since a single parameter can mislead. Record start-up and coast-down signatures when a machine is healthy so you have a baseline.
answers.q6: My mentor was a plant foreman who made me strip and rebuild a pump before I was allowed to write a recommendation. I carried that on by running monthly fault clinics where juniors present failed parts and diagnose them together.
answers.q7: I am handing over a reliability programme that moves our critical machines to condition-based overhaul, and a spares optimisation project. The risk is a shortage of skilled overhaul crews and delays in vendor spares, so long-lead items must be ordered early and local repair capability developed.
answers.q8: Learn to listen to machines and trust your senses as well as your instruments. Take every opportunity to strip and rebuild equipment with the technicians. Keep records of every overhaul and failure, because the history of a machine is its most valuable asset.

answers.q1: I began in personnel administration at a large asset and grew into corporate talent management. I learnt that a workforce plan is a promise to the people as much as a spreadsheet. The defining period was managing large-scale recruitment alongside a wave of retirements.
answers.q2: The toughest challenge was integrating a large cohort of new recruits at a time when many experienced people were retiring. We designed a structured induction, rotation through field locations and a buddy system with senior mentors. Attrition in the first three years fell noticeably, and managers reported that new joiners became productive sooner.
answers.q3: I once introduced a new performance process with too little consultation, and employees saw it as imposed from headquarters. Adoption was poor and we had to relaunch it after a year. Since then I pilot every major policy in two or three locations and listen to the people who will use it before rolling it out.
answers.q4: People safety includes psychological safety. Employees in remote and hazardous locations need fair rosters, adequate rest and support for family concerns. Managers must be trained to notice stress and fatigue, because tired people make mistakes. Make sure every employee knows whom to approach, in confidence, when they are struggling.
answers.q5: Before any new policy, walk the shop floor and ask three people it will affect what could go wrong. Never announce a transfer or promotion without speaking to the person first. Consistency matters more than perfection: people accept hard decisions when they believe the process was fair.
answers.q6: My first manager taught me to listen before I wrote any policy. I passed it on by pairing every new HR executive with a field visit to an installation, so they understood who their policies served.
answers.q7: I am handing over a succession framework that identifies critical roles and ready-now successors, but it needs annual refresh and honest conversations with employees. The biggest risk is that knowledge in retiring experts is not captured early enough. Start that process at least two years before retirement.
answers.q8: Be curious about operations. An HR professional who has never seen a rig, a plant or a seismic crew will struggle to design policies that work. Treat every employee conversation as an opportunity to learn something about the business.

answers.q1: I began as a safety officer on an offshore installation and spent three decades moving through process safety, audits, incident investigation and corporate HSE. The defining moment was investigating a serious incident early in my career and speaking with the family of an injured colleague. It convinced me that every procedure is written for a real person.
answers.q2: Our toughest challenge was reducing repeat incidents involving lifting operations on offshore platforms. We analysed three years of near-misses and found that most involved unclear communication between crane operator and rigger. We introduced standard hand signals, pre-lift briefings and mandatory observation by a second person. Lifting incidents fell sharply within eighteen months.
answers.q3: Early in my HSE career I treated audits as a tick-box exercise and issued long lists of findings that nobody read. Real improvement began when I shortened reports to three priority actions with named owners and follow-up dates.
answers.q4: Permit to work is the single most important barrier in our industry. Read the permit, walk the site and talk to the people doing the job before you sign. Stop-work authority belongs to everyone. Report near-misses without blame, because they are free lessons.
answers.q5: Walk the site at an odd hour, such as the end of a night shift, and look at the housekeeping, the permits on the board and the way people talk to each other. If workarounds are common, a procedure is probably unworkable. Count how many people can tell you the nearest muster point without thinking; that number reveals your safety culture.
answers.q6: My mentor was a senior safety manager who insisted I accompany him on every incident investigation and always asked why five times. I pass this on by taking young HSE officers on joint audits and asking them to lead the closing meeting with the unit head, so they build the confidence to speak up on safety.
answers.q7: I am handing over a programme to make contractor safety management consistent across all assets, and a digital system to track permits and near-misses. The risk is fatigue and cost pressure on contractors, so supervision must not be reduced. Keep up leadership site visits and recognise people who stop jobs.
answers.q8: Do not be the person who only says no. Learn the operation well enough to propose a safer way of doing the job. People respect a safety professional who understands their work.

answers.q1: I started as a fire officer in a plant and moved through offshore installations and terminals, eventually heading fire services. The defining moment was my first major fire as a junior officer, where the discipline of the team under pressure taught me that training, not courage, saves lives.
answers.q2: A hydrocarbon leak fire on a process facility tested our emergency response. Quick isolation, correct foam application and well-rehearsed roles contained it with no injuries. The after-action review showed that two hours of weekly drills were why people knew exactly what to do.
answers.q3: In a drill I once assumed a fire pump would start because it had passed its monthly test. It failed because of a clogged strainer, and the drill exposed it. In a real emergency the consequences could have been severe. I now insist on full-flow tests, a record of strainer cleaning and a backup plan for every critical pump.
answers.q4: Know your muster point, your escape routes and your role before an emergency starts. Fire teams cannot save a facility where permits are ignored and fire pumps are untested. Test fire water systems on schedule and record the results honestly.
answers.q5: Check the wind direction before you decide your approach to a gas leak or fire. Foam stocks, pump pressures and hose conditions should be inspected by touch and eye, not just by checklist. A fire crew that knows every valve on the facility will respond faster than any procedure.
answers.q6: My mentor was a chief fire officer who made me spend a month on every shift and learn each person's role. I pass it on through crew-led drills where junior firefighters play incident commander and seniors act as support, and by sharing lessons from each real incident across all stations.
answers.q7: I am handing over the modernisation of fire water systems at two terminals, a drone-based thermal inspection trial and a succession plan for station officers. The risk is ageing firefighting equipment and the difficulty of recruiting trained firefighters, so training academies and equipment replacement must stay a priority.
answers.q8: Train for the worst day, not the average day. Take part in drills as if they were real, give honest feedback and fix the weak points straight away. Learn the layout of every facility you protect, down to the location of each valve and hydrant, and walk it at night. Respect the older firefighters and ask them for their stories, because every old incident holds a lesson that no manual has recorded.

answers.q1: I began as a process engineer in gas processing and spent most of my career at a large plant receiving gas and condensate from offshore. A plant is a living system. I learnt that every modification, however small, must pass a proper management of change review.
answers.q2: A severe problem was unstable operation of the fractionation train after feed composition changed. We reviewed the control strategy, retuned loops and adjusted reflux ratios with the licensor's support. Product quality stabilised and flaring dropped markedly.
answers.q3: I once approved a plant start-up after a shutdown without personally checking that all blinds had been removed from a line. The unit tripped on low flow and, luckily, nothing worse happened. Since then I walk the critical lines with the shift in charge and insist on a signed blind list before every start-up, regardless of schedule pressure.
answers.q4: Respect the relief and flare system. Never assume a relief valve will protect you if it has not been tested or if upstream changes have increased the load. Run HAZOP reviews seriously and track every action to closure. Loss of containment is the event we must never accept.
answers.q5: Watch the trends of reflux drum level, column differential pressure and flare flow, because they warn you before alarms do. If the flare flame changes colour or size without a reason, find out why immediately. Keep a close eye on feed composition, because a small change can destabilise the plant within hours.
answers.q6: I learnt plant operations from a veteran shift superintendent who made me spend nights in the control room for a whole year. I now run mentoring pairs where young engineers shadow senior operators, and I hold monthly sessions where operators explain the logic behind each control loop.
answers.q7: I am handing over a modernisation of the control system and a flare-reduction project that still needs final tie-ins. The main risk is ageing equipment in the older units. Keep inspection plans funded even when budgets are tight.
answers.q8: Spend your early years in the control room and on the plant, not only in the office. Respect the operators, because they know the plant better than any drawing. Never skip a management of change review, however small the modification looks.

answers.q1: I joined in 1993 as a process engineer at the gas processing complex and worked on sweetening units, dehydration and condensate fractionation. Through two major expansions and many shutdowns I rose to lead the plant. The defining moment was commissioning a new unit, where I learnt that a good start-up depends on months of preparation by every discipline.
answers.q2: Our toughest challenge was a major turnaround of a sour gas processing unit where the amine system had suffered heavy corrosion. We re-planned the shutdown around inspection findings, pre-fabricated spools and rehearsed critical lifts. The unit returned to service within the planned window and with improved reliability.
answers.q3: I once accepted a vendor's assurance that a replacement amine pump was identical to the old one. It had a different curve and caused unstable circulation after start-up, so we had to shut down and replace it again. I now verify every replacement against data sheets and hold a proper review before accepting any substitute.
answers.q4: Hydrogen sulphide is the silent killer. Every person entering a sour area must carry a personal monitor and know the escape route and wind direction. Breathing apparatus must be inspected and drills held regularly. Never enter a confined space without a valid permit, gas test and standby person, and never go in to rescue without protection.
answers.q5: During start-up, never rush the first hour. Walk every line you have opened, check blinds and spades against the isolation list and confirm instrument calibration. For amine systems, watch foaming indicators and keep antifoam handy. Corrosion trends in the amine circuit tell you about problems months before failure.
answers.q6: My mentor was a senior plant manager who took me through every unit on night shift and made me explain what could go wrong. I pass that on by holding hazard walks with young engineers, and by asking each of them to prepare a one-page lesson after every shutdown.
answers.q7: I am handing over a debottlenecking study for the condensate fractionation section and a plan to upgrade the sulphur recovery unit. The risk is that contractors for the next shutdown will need to be locked in well ahead. Start planning at least eighteen months before the shutdown.
answers.q8: Learn to read a P&ID until you can draw it from memory. Spend time with operators on night shift and respect their experience. A plant engineer earns trust by being present during the difficult hours.
